client: I've been really stressed out lately because of this new job I started at a tech startup, and honestly it's been a lot more intense than I expected. Last week I missed an important deadline and I just can't stop thinking about it — like it plays on a loop in my head. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the pressure is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — the stress in your words comes through clearly, and even the way you're speaking, quickly and quietly, suggests you might be feeling a kind of overwhelmed tension that you're trying to hold together. That thought loop about the missed deadline is really common when our minds are trying to "solve" something, but it often just keeps us stuck in self-criticism rather than moving forward. And you're right that the pressure won't disappear when you leave here — but what we *can* work on is changing how your mind responds to that pressure, so it doesn't feel quite so relentless.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I mean... I hear what you're saying, but I guess I'm skeptical that changing how I "respond" to the pressure is really going to matter when my manager is literally watching every move I make. Like, the missed deadline was real, the consequences were real, and my coworkers definitely noticed. I don't know if reframing my thoughts is going to change any of that.
therapist: Your skepticism makes complete sense, and I want to validate that — the deadline, your manager's scrutiny, your coworkers noticing, those are all real and I'm not trying to minimize them. But I'm also noticing something in how you're speaking — there's a kind of quiet intensity there, like you're carrying something heavier than just the facts of what happened, almost like the situation has become a verdict about *you* as a person. The goal isn't to pretend the pressure isn't real, but to examine whether the story your mind is telling you about what it all *means* — about your worth, your competence — is as accurate as it feels right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... okay, maybe there's something to that. It does feel like more than just one missed deadline — like it's proof that I don't actually belong there, that I got lucky getting the job and now everyone's going to figure that out. But I'm not sure how you separate the "story" from the reality, because from where I'm standing it all feels like the same thing.
therapist: What you just described — that fear of being "found out," that the job was luck and not ability — has a name in CBT, it's called impostor syndrome, and the fact that your voice sounds a little rushed and tense right now tells me this hits somewhere really deep for you. Here's a gentle challenge though: what's the actual evidence that you *don't* belong there, versus the evidence that got you hired and has kept you there until now? Separating the story from reality starts with exactly that — not dismissing the feeling, but asking whether the facts actually support the conclusion your mind has jumped to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess when I actually try to think about it... I did go through four rounds of interviews, and they chose me over other candidates. But it's hard to hold onto that because one bad thing happens and it just wipes out all of that in my head, like the missed deadline carries way more weight than anything else. And honestly, trying to list "evidence" feels a bit clinical to me — like my brain isn't going to just accept a pros and cons list when it's in full panic mode.
therapist: You just did something really important there — you found real, concrete evidence of your competence, even if your mind immediately tried to push it away, and I notice you're speaking quickly and with a kind of high-strung energy that suggests part of you is still in that panic mode even as we talk. You're absolutely right that a neat list won't calm a brain that's in fight-or-flight, and that's not a flaw in you — it's just how anxiety works, it hijacks our ability to hold onto good information. So rather than fighting that with logic alone, we might focus on first helping your nervous system settle a little, so that the evidence you *already found* actually has a chance to land.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Okay, so when you say "help my nervous system settle" — are we talking about like breathing exercises or something? Because I've tried that before and I always feel kind of ridiculous doing it, especially at work where someone could walk by and see me. I do get what you're saying about the panic mode thing though, because it's true that even right now I'm half-thinking about what my manager might be thinking about me instead of actually being here.
therapist: That moment of self-awareness you just had — noticing that you're half-here and half-in your manager's head — is actually more powerful than any breathing exercise, and it's exactly the kind of skill we'd be building on. Your voice sounds quite quiet and a little strained right now, like you're working hard to stay composed while still being pulled in different directions, which makes complete sense given everything you're holding. And I hear you on the breathing thing feeling awkward — there are much more subtle ways to interrupt that panic cycle that wouldn't look like anything to a coworker walking by, so let's find something that actually fits your world.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Okay, I'm curious what those subtle things actually look like, because I'm willing to try something if it's not going to make me feel self-conscious on top of everything else. But I'll be honest — even if I learn some technique, I'm worried I'll forget to use it in the moment when things actually get intense, like when my manager calls me into a last-minute meeting and my heart just drops. That's when I really need it, but that's also exactly when I go blank.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — soft but fast, with a kind of high-pitched tension — really captures that feeling of bracing for something, like part of you is already rehearsing that moment your manager calls you in. What you're describing is actually really common: techniques fail us precisely when we need them most because we haven't yet built them into a *habit*, so the goal isn't to remember a technique under pressure but to practice it so many times in low-stakes moments that it becomes almost automatic. Something as simple as pressing your feet into the floor for two seconds — completely invisible to anyone around you — can interrupt that "going blank" response, and if we practice connecting that action to those specific triggers like the last-minute meeting, your brain starts to reach for it without you having to think.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The feet on the floor thing actually sounds doable, like I could see myself doing that without anyone noticing. But I guess my worry is that two seconds of pressing my feet down isn't really going to stop the spiral once it's already started — like when my manager says "can we chat?" my mind has already jumped ten steps ahead to worst-case scenarios before I've even stood up from my chair. Is that kind of thing actually going to be enough to interrupt something that moves that fast?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, with a kind of high, tight energy — really matches what you're describing, that lightning-fast jump to worst-case scenarios that feels almost impossible to catch in time. You're right that two seconds alone won't stop a spiral that's already moving at full speed, but the feet-on-the-floor isn't meant to stop the spiral — it's meant to create a tiny pause *before* your mind fully commits to the worst-case story, just enough of a gap to ask "is 'can we chat' actually a threat, or is that my anxiety filling in the blanks?" That question alone — practiced enough times — can start to slow down how automatically your brain races to catastrophe.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I think I actually understand the logic there — it's not about stopping the spiral but just creating a little gap, which feels more realistic than expecting myself to suddenly stay calm. But I'm still not sure I trust myself to ask that question in the moment, like "is this actually a threat" — because what if it IS actually a threat, what if my manager really is unhappy with me, and I'm just using the technique to talk myself out of something I should be taking seriously? I don't want to gaslight myself into thinking everything's fine when maybe it isn't.
therapist: That's actually a really sophisticated and honest concern, and the fact that you're thinking about it this carefully — even while speaking quickly and with that soft, high tension in your voice — tells me you're genuinely trying to engage with this rather than just looking for an easy out. The technique was never meant to convince you everything is fine — it's meant to help you respond *thoughtfully* instead of *reactively*, so that if your manager really is unhappy with you, you can actually have a productive conversation about it rather than shutting down or spiraling. There's a real difference between grounding yourself to see clearly and gaslighting yourself into denial — one helps you face reality better, the other avoids it, and what you're describing sounds much more like someone who wants to face things clearly.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That distinction actually helps — responding thoughtfully versus reactively, I think I can hold onto that. I guess what I'm realizing is that a big part of why the missed deadline hit so hard is that I already went into this job expecting to fail, so every little thing feels like confirmation. I'm just not sure how to change that underlying expectation, because it's been there a lot longer than this job has.
therapist: What you just named is really significant — that the expectation of failure came *first*, and the job is just the latest place it's showing up, and I notice your voice has this soft, almost careful quality right now, like you're handling something fragile that you've maybe never quite put into words before. That underlying belief — "I'm going to fail, it's only a matter of time" — is exactly what CBT calls a core belief, and you're right that it's much older and deeper than one missed deadline or one job. The good news is that it *is* changeable, not quickly or easily, but the fact that you can already see it clearly enough to name it means you've already taken the hardest first step.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, it's weird to actually say it out loud like that, because I think I've always kind of known it was there but never really looked at it directly. It's almost a relief to name it, but also kind of scary, because if this is a "core belief" that's been running in the background my whole life, that feels like a really big thing to try to change — like, where do you even start with something that deep? I guess I'm worried we'll open this up and I won't be able to actually do anything about it in the time I have.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, with a kind of high, stretched quality — really captures that mix of relief and fear you're describing, like something has been uncovered that feels both freeing and overwhelming at the same time. I want to gently push back on the worry that we've opened something too big to handle though — you don't change a core belief by attacking it all at once, you change it through exactly what you've already been doing today, noticing it, questioning it, finding small moments where the evidence doesn't actually support it. You've already started, and that's not nothing — that's everything.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
